raw_text:
### Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review of Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Therapeutics

#### Introduction
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded, insoluble amyloid fibrils within the myocardium [1]. While historically considered a rare and terminal condition, advances in diagnostic imaging and serum biomarker assays have shown that CA is a major and underdiagnosed cause of heart failure (HF), particularly in older adults [1]. The clinical landscape is dominated by two primary systemic types: light-chain amyloidosis (AL) and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), which is further classified into hereditary (variant, ATTRv) and wild-type (ATTRwt) forms [2,3]. Historically, the prognosis of CA was dismal; however, early detection combined with modern disease-modifying therapies has transformed it into a highly treatable disease [4].

#### Pathophysiology
The core mechanism of CA involves the misfolding of soluble precursor proteins into stable, insoluble β-sheet-rich fibrils that deposit in the myocardial extracellular space [5]. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia overproduces monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains that are intrinsically cardiotoxic, inducing rapid cellular damage alongside mechanical infiltration [2,6]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis involves the destabilization of the transthyretin (TTR) tetramer, a liver-synthesized transport protein [1]. Destabilization causes the tetramer to dissociate into rate-limiting, rate-determining amyloidogenic monomers [7]. In ATTRv, this is driven by pathogenic point mutations in the TTR gene, whereas ATTRwt occurs as an age-related, non-genetic process [7,8]. ATTRwt commonly manifests as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in elderly males [8].

#### Diagnostic Framework and Red Flags
Early and accurate diagnosis is critical, particularly because untreated AL amyloidosis carries a high risk of rapid clinical deterioration and death [2,4]. Clinicians must maintain high clinical suspicion and recognize extracardiac and cardiac "red flags." These clinical clues include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (often preceding cardiac symptoms by years), lumbar spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and a classic discordance between severe left ventricular wall thickening on echocardiography and low QRS voltage on electrocardiography [1,4,7].

Modern diagnostics rely heavily on a well-validated non-invasive pathway [3]. Transthoracic echocardiography typically reveals concentric ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and a classic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain [9]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is highly sensitive, demonstrating diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) alongside expanded extracellular volume (ECV) and elevated native T1 mapping values [10].

The cornerstone of the non-invasive diagnostic algorithm is the combination of technetium-99m (99mTc) bone-seeking radiotracer scintigraphy (using PYP, DPD, or HMDP) and a complete monoclonal protein screen [3,11]. As established by Gillmore et al., a grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy, in the absolute absence of a monoclonal protein in both serum and urine (verified via serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light chain assay), is 100% specific for ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, avoiding the need for an invasive endomyocardial biopsy [3,12]. If any monoclonal protein is detected, urgent tissue biopsy (or endomyocardial biopsy) with mass spectrometry-based typing is mandatory to exclude or confirm AL amyloidosis [2,4,13].

#### Therapeutics
The management of CA differs fundamentally between subtypes [4,12]. For AL amyloidosis, the therapeutic goal is rapid elimination of the hematotoxic plasma cell clone [2,13]. The current standard of care was established by the landmark ANDROMEDA trial, which demonstrated that adding the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab to the cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) regimen significantly increases rates of complete hematologic and organ response [14].

For ATTR amyloidosis, treatment aims to prevent further TTR amyloid deposition through stabilization or gene silencing [1]. The landmark ATTR-ACT trial showed that the TTR kinetic stabilizer tafamidis significantly reduces all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations in both ATTRwt and ATTRv patients [15]. Another stabilizer, acoramidis, has demonstrated robust efficacy and high-affinity stabilization in the ATTRibute-CM trial, further expanding therapeutic options [20].

An alternative strategy is gene silencing, which suppresses hepatic TTR synthesis [1,16]. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapies (patisiran, vutrisiran) and antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) (inotersen, eplontersen) have shown significant efficacy [16,17]. The APOLLO and NEURO-TTR trials originally validated these therapies in ATTRv polyneuropathy [16,17]. Subsequent trials, notably the APOLLO-B trial for patisiran, demonstrated preservation of functional capacity (measured by the 6-minute walk distance) and quality of life in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy [18,19]. ASO therapies like eplontersen (NEURO-TTRansform) continue to redefine management [21]. More recently, in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing therapies (e.g., NTLA-2001) are being investigated, offering the potential for a one-time curative treatment through durable knockout of the TTR gene [22].

#### Supportive Care and Prognosis
General supportive care remains vital but clinically challenging [1,24]. Standard HF therapies (e.g., beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors) are often poorly tolerated or contraindicated due to restrictive physiology and autonomic neuropathy [24,25]. Loop diuretics and aldosterone antagonists are the mainstay of volume management, while digitalis and calcium channel blockers are contraindicated due to their binding risk to amyloid fibrils [24]. Autonomic dysfunction and high-risk arrhythmias must be managed carefully [25,26].

While cardiac amyloidosis was previously viewed as a terminal illness [26,27], earlier diagnosis and aggressive disease-modifying therapies have vastly improved the clinical trajectory and survival rates for both AL and ATTR patients [28,30]. Novel therapies aiming to clear existing amyloid deposits, such as anti-SAP antibodies or other fibril disruptors, are actively being investigated and may soon provide pathways for actual disease regression [29].
